title: Molecular basis of life. Nucleic acids and their role in passing hereditary traits from generation to generation. The role of DNA in protein biosynthesis. Genetic engineering. Variability and its forms

goals.text: To teach the student the evidence that DNA is the hereditary material, the structure and replication of nucleic acids, the properties of the genetic code, the stages of transcription and translation, the regulation of gene activity, the basics of gene and cell engineering, and the forms of variability and the classification of mutations.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the essence of the experiments on transformation, transduction and conjugation;
the structure of DNA and RNA, Chargaff’s rules and the semiconservative mode of replication;
the properties of the genetic code and the stages of protein biosynthesis;
the operon theory (induction and repression);
the types of variability, the classification of mutations, DNA repair and antimutagens.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the complementary strand, mRNA and amino acid sequence from a DNA strand;
calculate the percentage of nucleotides using Chargaff’s rule;
identify the type of mutation from a description or a diagram.

sections.title: 1. Proof that DNA is the hereditary material

F. Griffith (1928), O. Avery and colleagues (1944)

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: F. Griffith's experiment (1928): mice survive when given live unencapsulated R-strain or heat-killed S-strain alone, but die when given live S-strain or the mixture of the two — the virulence trait passed from dead S-bacteria to live R-bacteria (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In Griffith's experiment the nature of the “transforming principle” remained unknown. In 1944 **O. Avery, C. MacLeod and M. McCarty** separated protein, polysaccharide and DNA from the S-strain and showed that only **DNA** turned the R-strain into the S-strain, and that this ability was lost after treatment with DNase. This was the first direct proof that DNA is the hereditary material.

**Plasmids** are small circular DNA molecules in bacteria outside the chromosome; they replicate independently. The F plasmid ensures conjugation, and R plasmids provide **antibiotic resistance** and spread rapidly between bacteria. Plasmids are used as **vectors** in genetic engineering.

sections.title: 2. Structure of nucleic acids and DNA replication

blocks.text: Nucleic acids are biopolymers built of **nucleotides**. Each nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a pentose (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) and a phosphate residue. Nitrogenous bases: **purines** — adenine (A) and guanine (G); **pyrimidines** — cytosine (C), thymine (T, only in DNA) and uracil (U, only in RNA).

In 1953 **J. Watson and F. Crick** proposed the double helix model of DNA (based on the X-ray diffraction data of R. Franklin and M. Wilkins). DNA consists of two **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′) polynucleotide strands; the strands are joined by hydrogen bonds between nitrogenous bases according to the principle of **complementarity**: A=T (2 hydrogen bonds), G≡C (3 hydrogen bonds). The helix diameter is 2 nm, one turn contains 10 nucleotide pairs, the pitch is 3.4 nm and the distance between neighboring nucleotides is 0.34 nm (Figure 6.2).

blocks.label: Figure 6.2

parts.text: **Chargaff’s rules:** A = T, G = C; the sum of purines equals the sum of pyrimidines (A + G = T + C). So if you know the percentage of one base in DNA, you can calculate the others: for example, if G = 20 %, then C = 20 % and A = T = 30 %.

blocks.text: **Replication** is the self-duplication of DNA; it takes place in the S period of interphase. M. Meselson and F. Stahl (1958) proved that replication is **semiconservative**: each new DNA molecule has one old (template) strand and one new strand. In the process **helicase** unwinds the double helix, **topoisomerase** relieves the twisting, **primase** synthesizes an RNA primer and **DNA polymerase** builds the new strand only in the 5′→3′ direction; therefore one strand is made continuously (leading) and the other as Okazaki fragments (lagging), which are joined by **ligase**.

blocks.label: Figure 6.3
blocks.caption: Scheme of the Meselson–Stahl experiment: parental molecules and first- and second-generation DNA molecules — the semi-conservative, conservative and dispersive models of replication (1, 2, 3) compared (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Meselson and Stahl grew *E. coli* on heavy nitrogen (^15^N) medium and then moved it to ordinary nitrogen (^14^N) medium. In the first generation all DNA had **intermediate density** (^15^N/^14^N); in the second generation half was intermediate and half light. This result fits only the semi-conservative model.

blocks.label: Figure 6.4
blocks.caption: The replication fork: helicase separates the strands, topoisomerase relieves tension, primase makes an RNA primer, DNA polymerase synthesises the leading strand continuously and the lagging strand as Okazaki fragments, and DNA ligase joins them (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 6.4. Enzymes and proteins taking part in replication
head: Enzyme (protein)
Function
rows: Breaks hydrogen bonds and “unzips” the double helix
Removes the twisting tension created as the helix unwinds
Keep the separated single strands from re-joining
Synthesises a short RNA primer to which the polymerase adds nucleotides
Builds the new strand only in the 5′→3′ direction and proofreads errors
Joins Okazaki fragments with a phosphodiester bond

blocks.text: Because DNA polymerase works only in the 5′→3′ direction, the two strands are built differently: the **leading strand** is made continuously in the direction of fork movement, and the **lagging strand** in the opposite direction as short pieces — **Okazaki fragments** (100–200 nucleotides in eukaryotes). In a eukaryotic chromosome replication starts at thousands of points (**replicons**) at once, so the huge DNA is doubled in a few hours.

sections.title: 3. The genetic code and protein biosynthesis

blocks.text: The **genetic code** is the system of recording the amino acid sequence of a protein by the nucleotide sequence of mRNA. Its properties:

items: **Triplet** — each amino acid is coded by three nucleotides (a codon); there are 4^3^ = 64 codons, 61 of which code amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are **stop codons**.
**Degeneracy (redundancy)** — most amino acids are coded by several codons (only methionine and tryptophan by one each).
**Unambiguity (specificity)** — each codon specifies only one amino acid.
**Continuity and non-overlapping** — there are no “commas” between codons, and one nucleotide does not belong to two codons.
**Universality** — the code is almost the same in all organisms.
**Start codon** — AUG (methionine).

Codons

blocks.text: **Transcription** is the synthesis of mRNA on one (template) strand of DNA by RNA polymerase (Figure 6.5). It starts at the promoter and ends at the terminator. In eukaryotes pre-mRNA is formed first; during **processing** a “cap” is added to the 5′ end and a poly-A “tail” to the 3′ end, and in **splicing** introns are cut out and exons are joined.

blocks.label: Figure 6.5
blocks.caption: Diagram of transcription: RNA polymerase opens the DNA double helix and synthesizes an RNA strand complementary to the template strand (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 6.6. Types of RNA

Share in the cell
Function

Regulate gene activity by degrading mRNA or blocking translation

blocks.text: **Structure of a eukaryotic gene.** At the start of the gene is the **promoter** (TATA box) where RNA polymerase binds, then alternating **exons** (protein-coding parts) and **introns** (non-coding parts), and at the end the **terminator**. More distant **enhancers** boost transcription. In splicing the introns are cut out and the exons joined; joining the exons of one gene in different ways (**alternative splicing**) allows several different proteins to be made from one gene. Only ≈ 1,5 % of the human genome codes for protein.

**Translation** is the synthesis of a polypeptide chain on the ribosome according to the information in mRNA (Figure 6.7). Amino acids are activated by special enzymes (aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases) and attached to tRNA. The **anticodon** of tRNA binds to the mRNA codon by complementarity.

blocks.label: Figure 6.6
blocks.caption: Secondary structure of alanine tRNA (“cloverleaf”): the amino acid attaches to the 3′ end, and the anticodon in the lower loop pairs complementarily with the mRNA codon (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

items: **Initiation** — the small ribosomal subunit binds to mRNA, the tRNA carrying methionine takes its place at the start codon AUG, and then the large subunit joins.
**Elongation** — the next aminoacyl-tRNA arrives at the A site, a peptide bond forms between the amino acids, and the ribosome moves one codon (translocation).
**Termination** — when the ribosome reaches a stop codon, the polypeptide is released and the ribosome dissociates into subunits.

blocks.label: Figure 6.7
blocks.caption: Stages of protein biosynthesis (translation): initiation, elongation and termination; small and large ribosomal subunits, tRNA and mRNA (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Many antibiotics stop bacterial translation: tetracyclines (binding of tRNA), streptomycin (the small subunit), chloramphenicol and macrolides (the large subunit). They act selectively on the 70S ribosomes of bacteria.

sections.title: 4. Regulation of gene activity and cytoplasmic heredity

blocks.text: F. Jacob and J. Monod (1961) created the **operon** theory in Escherichia coli. An operon is a group of structural genes transcribed together under one promoter and operator. A regulator gene synthesizes a **repressor** protein, which binds to the operator and blocks the movement of RNA polymerase.

items: **Induction** (lactose operon): without lactose in the medium the repressor is bound to the operator and the genes are off; lactose (the inducer) binds and inactivates the repressor — enzymes that break down lactose are synthesized.
**Repression** (tryptophan operon): when the end product (tryptophan) accumulates, it activates the repressor as a corepressor and synthesis stops.

blocks.text: In eukaryotes gene activity is regulated at many levels: chromatin condensation (DNA methylation, histone modification), transcription factors and enhancers, splicing, mRNA stability and translation.

**Epigenetic regulation** is a heritable change in gene activity without a change in the DNA nucleotide sequence. Its main mechanisms are cytosine **methylation** (a methylated promoter is “switched off”), acetylation and methylation of histones, and non-coding RNAs. **Genomic imprinting** means that for some genes only the copy from the father or only the copy from the mother works. For example, if the same region of chromosome 15 is lost on the paternal copy, **Prader–Willi syndrome** (obesity, intellectual disability) develops; if it is lost on the maternal copy, **Angelman syndrome** (seizures, unprovoked laughter) develops.

**Cytoplasmic (extranuclear) heredity** is the inheritance of traits through the DNA of mitochondria and plastids. In humans mitochondria pass to the zygote only through the egg, so mitochondrial diseases (Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, MELAS) are passed **only from the mother** to all her children.
**Genetic engineering** is the set of methods for isolating desired genes, transferring them into the cells of another organism with a vector and using them. Its main stages:

items: Obtaining the desired gene — cutting DNA with **restriction enzymes** (for example, EcoRI) or synthesizing complementary DNA from mRNA with reverse transcriptase.
Joining the gene into a **vector** (plasmid, bacteriophage, virus) with **ligase** — forming recombinant DNA.
Introducing the recombinant DNA into a recipient cell (bacterium, yeast).
Selecting and multiplying (cloning) the cells that received the gene and isolating the product.

blocks.label: Figure 6.8
blocks.caption: Action of the restriction enzyme EcoRI: the enzyme recognises the sequence GAATTC and cuts both strands in a staggered way, forming “sticky ends”; these ends pair complementarily with other DNA cut by the same enzyme (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Genetic engineering is used to produce **human insulin**, growth hormone, interferons, hepatitis B vaccine and blood clotting factors; **gene therapy**, transgenic plants and animals, PCR (polymerase chain reaction) diagnosis and genome editing with CRISPR-Cas9 are developing.
The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

PCR (K. Mullis, 1983) is a method of multiplying a desired piece of DNA millions of times in a test tube. Template DNA, two **primers** (short strands complementary to the ends of the region to be copied), the four nucleotides and heat-stable **Taq polymerase** are added to the reaction mixture. Each cycle has three steps and doubles the amount of DNA: 30 cycles give 2^30^ ≈ 1 billion copies.

items: **Denaturation** (94–95 °C) — the DNA strands separate.
**Primer annealing** (50–65 °C) — the primers bind complementarily to the template.
**Elongation** (72 °C) — Taq polymerase builds the new strand starting from the primer.

parts.text: PCR is widely used in medicine: detection of infections (SARS-CoV-2, HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, tuberculosis), DNA diagnosis of hereditary diseases and carrier status, prenatal diagnosis, forensic identification and paternity testing (DNA “fingerprints”) and molecular diagnosis of tumours.

blocks.text: **Cell engineering** is growing cells, hybridizing them (somatic hybridization) and cloning by nuclear transfer. **Hybridomas** obtained by fusing a lymphocyte with a tumor cell produce monoclonal antibodies. The sheep “Dolly” was cloned by nuclear transfer in 1996.

blocks.text: By the site of origin, **somatic** mutations (in body cells — not inherited, cause tumors and mosaicism) and **generative** mutations (in sex cells — passed to offspring) are distinguished. By cause, there are **spontaneous** (natural, cause unknown) and **induced** (under the action of mutagens) mutations. Mutagens: **physical** (ionizing and ultraviolet radiation, high temperature), **chemical** (alkylating agents, nitrous acid, benzopyrene, some drugs), **biological** (viruses, mobile genetic elements).

**DNA repair** is the system that restores damaged DNA: **photoreactivation** (splitting thymine dimers in light), **excision repair** (cutting out the damaged segment and rebuilding it with DNA polymerase and ligase) and **postreplicative repair**. If repair fails, mutations accumulate: for example, in **xeroderma pigmentosum** ultraviolet light causes skin cancer. **Antimutagens** are substances that reduce the frequency of mutations: vitamins (A, E, C), selenium, some amino acids, antioxidants.

parts.text: **Sickle cell anemia** is a classic point mutation: the substitution GAG → GTG in codon 6 of the β-globin gene puts valine in place of glutamic acid (HbS). At low oxygen HbS polymerizes, the erythrocyte takes a sickle shape and blocks the capillaries.

blocks.text: **Antimutagens** are substances that reduce the frequency of mutations: antioxidants (vitamins C and E, β-carotene), some amino acids (cysteine), selenium and plant flavonoids. They bind free radicals and enhance repair.

**N.I. Vavilov's law of homologous series in hereditary variability (1920):** genetically close species and genera show similar series of hereditary variation. Therefore a mutation found in one species allows a similar mutation to be predicted in related species. In medicine this law underlies the creation of animal **models** of human hereditary diseases (haemophilia, albinism, muscular dystrophy).
Modification variability and the norm of reaction

The genotype determines not the trait itself but the range within which it can vary with the environment — the **norm of reaction**. Traits with a wide norm of reaction (body weight, muscle mass, skin tanning) change a lot with the environment, while traits with a narrow norm (eye colour, blood group) hardly change. Modifications are **group**, **adaptive** and **reversible**, and they are not inherited. They are studied statistically by building a **variation series**: from the variants (v) and their frequencies (p) the mean is found by the formula M = Σ(v · p) / n; its graph is the **variation curve** (normal distribution).

parts.text: **Xeroderma pigmentosum** is a hereditary deficiency (autosomal recessive) of the **excision repair** enzymes that cut out thymine dimers formed by UV light. Patients develop spots and ulcers on the skin after sunlight and skin cancer at a young age; they must be fully protected from sunlight.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The nucleotides of an mRNA are: guanine — 34 %, uracil — 18 %, cytosine — 28 %, adenine — 20 %.
cases.ask: Determine the percentage of nitrogenous bases in the double-stranded DNA segment from which this mRNA was copied.
cases.answer: The template DNA strand is complementary to the mRNA: C — 34 %, A — 18 %, G — 28 %, T — 20 %. The second (coding) strand is similar to the mRNA (T instead of U): G — 34 %, T — 18 %, C — 28 %, A — 20 %. In double-stranded DNA: G = C = (34 + 28) / 2 = 31 %; A = T = (18 + 20) / 2 = 19 %. Check: 31 + 31 + 19 + 19 = 100 %.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: The template strand of DNA is: ACC-ATA-GTC-CAA-GGA-CCA-AAC-AGA-AAA-TTT.
cases.ask: Which amino acids make up the polypeptide synthesized from this segment?
cases.answer: mRNA: UGG-UAU-CAG-GUU-CCU-GGU-UUG-UCU-UUU-AAA. Polypeptide: tryptophan — tyrosine — glutamine — valine — proline — glycine — leucine — serine — phenylalanine — lysine.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a patient’s β-globin gene, the sequence GAG in triplet 6 was found to be replaced by GTG.
cases.ask: What kind of mutation is this, and what disease does it cause?
cases.answer: This is a gene (point) mutation — a base substitution (transversion A → T). In mRNA the codon GAG (glutamic acid) becomes GUG (valine); at position 6 of the β-globin chain valine stands instead of glutamic acid — hemoglobin S is formed. As a result sickle cell anemia develops (autosomal recessive); heterozygotes are relatively resistant to malaria.

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: In a laboratory, a single viral DNA molecule from a patient's blood was amplified by PCR. The reaction ran for 25 cycles.
cases.ask: How many DNA copies are formed in theory? What happens in each cycle?
cases.answer: Each cycle doubles the amount of DNA: 2^25^ = 33 554 432, that is ≈ 33,5 million copies. In each cycle: (1) **denaturation** at 94–95 °C — the strands separate; (2) **primer annealing** at 50–65 °C; (3) **elongation** at 72 °C — heat-stable Taq polymerase builds the new strands. This is why PCR can detect even a very small amount of a pathogen.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: The beginning of an mRNA is: AUG-UUU-GGC-AAA-CUG-UAA. A mutation deleted the first U of the second codon.
cases.ask: What peptide is made before and after the mutation? What kind of mutation is this?
cases.answer: Before the mutation: AUG (Met) – UUU (Phe) – GGC (Gly) – AAA (Lys) – CUG (Leu) – UAA (stop) → Met–Phe–Gly–Lys–Leu. After the deletion the mRNA is AUG-UUG-GCA-AAC-UGU-AA… → Met–Leu–Ala–Asn–Cys and so on — every amino acid after the first codon has changed and the stop codon is lost. This is a **frameshift** — a deletion of one nucleotide; the protein is usually completely non-functional.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: A 5-year-old child develops severe redness, pigment spots and ulcers on the skin even after a short time in the sun. The parents are healthy and are blood relatives.
cases.ask: What disease should be considered? What are its molecular mechanism and mode of inheritance?
cases.answer: This is **xeroderma pigmentosum**. UV light forms **thymine dimers** between neighbouring thymines in DNA; in a normal cell these are cut out by **excision repair** enzymes and the strand is rebuilt. In the patient these enzymes are hereditarily lacking, damage accumulates and mutations and skin cancer develop. The disease is **autosomal recessive**: the healthy parents are heterozygous carriers, and a consanguineous marriage increases the chance that the same recessive gene meets. Management is complete protection from the sun and early detection of tumours.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Flow of information (the central dogma): **DNA → RNA → protein**; in retroviruses reverse transcriptase also opens the route RNA → DNA.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Stop codons: **“U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away”** — UAA, UAG, UGA.

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: Products of genetic engineering are insulin, growth hormone, interferon and vaccines; PCR and genome editing are the basis of modern diagnosis and treatment.
